Manual

Host upgrade and restart while plugins run

Ilium can stop and start while your plugin has running instances. That happens when the user restarts Ilium, when the session server stops, after a crash, or after a reboot. This page says which of your instances keep running, which are stopped and why, what happens to calls that are still in flight, what survives, and what the operator does. It does not describe a plugin update. For that, see Compatibility and upgrades and Install, update and uninstall.

Short answer

Event Running instances Your code sees What survives
Clean server stop Stopped deactivate(shutdown) once per live instance, in reverse start order Storage, settings, grants, node metadata, durable timers. Restore bytes are kept only in the session snapshot for client sides
Server crash or kill Stopped without a call No deactivate Storage, settings and metadata as of the last durable write or snapshot. Server restore bytes are lost
Client process killed The client instance is gone No deactivate The last restore bytes the server stored for that client side
Host shutdown takes longer than 5 s Remaining plugins dropped No deactivate for the dropped plugins As for a crash, for those plugins
Plugin restart after a counted failure Restarted after 1 s, then 5 s deactivate is not sent after a trap Storage and settings. Linear memory is lost

Nothing runs after a restart until the host activates the plugin again. The host starts after the kernel has restored the session snapshot, and it activates plugins on their triggers. The exact activation order is in Lifecycle.

Keep running or stopped

  • All instances stop when the server stops. Linear memory and variables are lost in every case. This follows from the rule that an instance lives from activate until deactivate, a trap or a restart. See Runtime model.
  • A plugin that was enabled stays enabled. Its package state is stored on disk, and it survives a server restart and a reboot. See Plugin lifecycle states.
  • A plugin side that was stopped by failure stays stopped. The server side is stored in installed.json as failure_stopped, so it survives a server restart. A client or scene side is held only in memory and is dropped when its client detaches. See Plugin lifecycle states.
  • A restart timer that was scheduled is cancelled when the server stops. It is not carried over to the next start. See Plugin lifecycle states.
  • The failure metrics reset when the server restarts. See Health and watchdog.
  • [LIF-198] At the first start after the host version changes, the host MUST write one audit record host.upgraded with the previous and new host versions, the previous and new API windows, and the ids of every plugin whose state became Incompatible, before any plugin activates. (proposed, owner to confirm)

Deactivate reason and timeout

Case Reason sent Deadline Bytes kept
Server stop begins shutdown 500 ms by default, 1,000 ms ceiling for a T1 plugin Yes, for the next activation in the same server process only. A server restart drops them
Client detaches cleanly shutdown 500 ms by default Yes, sent to the server and stored in the session snapshot
Client process killed or crashed None sent None The last bytes the server stored
Plugin update or dev reload upgrade 500 ms by default Yes

A deactivate that misses its deadline drops the instance and discards its bytes. Its log line is deactivate.deadline. The plugin is not counted as failed. Restore bytes are limited to 1 MiB. A larger return is dropped, one warning line is logged, and the next activation gets no restored value.

The host gives the whole server shutdown 5 s. If it takes longer, the remaining plugins are dropped without deactivate, and the error host.shutdown-timeout is logged. See Errors and limits.

In-flight calls

  • A call that is pending when its instance is deactivated or dropped completes as cancelled. The host does not call into the instance for it. See Errors and limits.
  • A pending request is never saved. Pending requests are lost at every event in the persistence table, including a server restart.
  • cancelled is listed as a case where the call may or may not have taken effect. Retry only where the operation is safe to repeat. See Errors and limits.
  • A write that finishes during deactivate is kept only if it finishes within the deactivate deadline. See Persistence and restart.

In-flight calls after a crash

A server crash or a kill stops the process without a deactivate call. The calls that were pending at that moment are not saved, so the new activation never receives a completion for them. From your code's point of view, a write that was in flight has an unknown outcome: it may have reached storage, a file or a terminal, or it may not have. The host does not replay it, and no outcome code is produced for it, because no caller remains to receive one. (The cancelled code applies only to a clean shutdown, as the table above shows.)

The input-uncertain event of journaled send-input is the one case where the host tells the plugin about an unknown outcome. Every other write needs the procedure below.

  • [OPS-209] After a crash or a kill, a call that was pending at the moment of the stop MUST NOT complete for the new activation, MUST NOT be replayed by the host, and MUST NOT be reported with the code cancelled, because only a clean shutdown produces that code. The host MUST NOT store pending calls durably to make this known. Test: give a fixture plugin one pending fs write, kill the server during the call, start the server, and assert that the new activation receives no completion for that call and that the file was not written a second time. (proposed, owner to confirm)
  • [OPS-210] A plugin that makes a write MUST first store its intent in its own data storage under a key it chooses, with a unique idempotency key for that write, and MUST mark the intent as done only after the write returns ok. Test: write an intent, kill the server before the write returns, restart, and assert that the intent is still stored and not marked as done. (proposed, owner to confirm)
  • [OPS-211] On each activation, a plugin MUST read every intent that is not marked as done, MUST check the target state that the write would have changed, and MUST repeat the write only when that check shows the write did not apply. A plugin MUST NOT repeat a write whose check shows that it applied. Test: leave one intent whose write applied before a kill, restart, and assert that the plugin repeats no write and marks the intent as done. (proposed, owner to confirm)

State that survives

State Server restart Crash Notes
Linear memory and variables Lost Lost Never saved
Restore bytes (server side) Lost Lost Kept in memory only
Restore bytes (client side) Not applicable, the client reconnects and keeps them Last stored bytes kept Stored in the session snapshot
Global storage bucket Kept As of last durable write
Project storage bucket Kept As of last durable write
Session storage bucket Kept only for the open session As of last durable write
Settings, grants, node metadata Kept As of last durable write
Durable timers and journal Kept As of last durable write

The table is the same as the one in Persistence and restart. Use it as the reference. Write your restore bytes only for state that cannot be stored in storage, because they do not survive a crash.

Your code after a restart

  • Do not assume that a restored value is there. Restore bytes reach activate only when the stored data_version matches the build that wrote them. Check the first byte and fall back to defaults when it is not a format you know. See Compatibility and upgrades.
  • Treat storage as the source of truth. Write each change to storage as it happens, not only in deactivate.
  • Make activate idempotent. It can run again after any restart, after a restart timer, or after a crash.
  • Do not rely on a deactivate reason to detect that Ilium restarted. shutdown is also used for a client detach.

Operator steps

Use these steps after a host upgrade or a restart when a plugin does not behave as expected.

  1. Run ilium plugin list --json to read the package state and the side states of each plugin. The state is installed-enabled, stopped-by-failure or another value from Plugin lifecycle states.
  2. Read the log with ilium plugin logs <id> --tail 100. Look for deactivate.deadline, host.shutdown-timeout, restart.scheduled and update.rolled-back.
  3. If a plugin is stopped-by-failure, fix the cause and enable it again. Enabling clears its failure window. See Lifecycle.
  4. For a plugin update that went wrong, use ilium plugin rollback <id>. Rollback follows the data rules of Install, update and uninstall, and --restore-backup or --discard-data may be needed.

Open decisions

These points are not established by the manual's current sources. Each one needs a decision before a requirement can be written for it. Each item states its owner, its deadline and the default that applies until it is decided. The sources name no owner and set no deadline for these items, so the release review assigns the owner and sets the date. A default marked "proposed, not agreed" is this page's suggestion and is not in force.

The three items about the Ilium binary, the restart command and host rollback now have an operator procedure, its requirements (LIF-295 to LIF-298) and the decisions it needs, in Upgrading Ilium and rolling back the host. The other items are still open.

  • Requirement ids. The ids HST-300 to HST-305 are already used by Performance budgets and benchmarks, and the register Requirements: kernel and host lists them. The file reference-requirements-host-platform.md named for this page does not exist. Choice: assign a new unused range for host restart requirements in the kernel and host register. Consequence: until then this page has no requirement ids, and its rules are not tested. Owner: not named; the release review assigns one. Deadline: none set; needed before the restart rules are tested. Default until decided: none. This page keeps no requirement ids.
  • Ilium binary upgrade. The sources describe a plugin update and a dev reload. They do not describe what happens to running plugins when the Ilium binary itself is replaced. Choice: document the swap as a host restart, which stops every instance with shutdown, or document a separate path. Consequence: operators need to know whether plugins keep running on the old binary until the next restart. See Upgrading Ilium and rolling back the host for the procedure and the decision it needs. Owner: not named; the release review assigns one. Deadline: none set; needed before the operator steps for a binary replacement are released. Default until decided: none agreed. Proposed, not agreed: a binary replacement is a server stop, so the clean-stop row of the short answer applies.
  • Who restarts Ilium. The manual does not say which command restarts the server, or whether a restart is done by the user alone. Choice: name the supported restart command in the operator steps. Consequence: the steps above cannot name one command yet. See Upgrading Ilium and rolling back the host for the procedure and the decision it needs. Owner: not named; the release review assigns one. Deadline: none set; needed before the operator steps are released. Default until decided: none. The operator steps name no restart command.
  • Failure window across a server restart. The window is per plugin, side, scope and version (Lifecycle). The sources do not say whether a window is kept across a server restart or reset. Choice: keep the window in memory and reset it, as the metrics do, or store it like failure_stopped. Consequence: a plugin that failed twice before a restart may get the full restart rule again, or may stay one failure from being disabled. Owner: not named; the release review assigns one. Deadline: none set; needed before the restart rule of Errors and limits is tested across a restart. Default until decided: none agreed. Proposed, not agreed: the window resets with the failure metrics.
  • Ilium rollback. ilium plugin rollback covers plugin versions only. The sources do not describe rolling back Ilium itself. Choice: state that the plugin rollback does not change the host, or describe a host rollback once it exists. Consequence: operators could assume that rolling back a plugin also undoes a host change. See Upgrading Ilium and rolling back the host for the procedure and the decision it needs. Owner: not named; the release review assigns one. Deadline: none set; needed before the rollback steps of the operator procedure are released. Default until decided: none agreed. Proposed, not agreed: a plugin rollback changes no host file.
  • Pending requests on a crash. The persistence table says pending requests are lost, and the errors table says cancelled on shutdown. The sources do not say what a caller sees after a crash, where no cancelled is produced. Choice: document the caller's view after a crash as a lost call with an unknown outcome. Consequence: plugins that submit writes must check their result after activation. Owner: not named; the release review assigns one. Deadline: none set; needed before the caller-side rule in Errors and limits is tested. Default until decided: none agreed. Proposed, not agreed: after a crash the caller sees a lost call with an unknown outcome, and no cancelled is produced. The section In-flight calls after a crash sets out this proposal as rules OPS-209 to OPS-211, which the owner still has to confirm.

Unconfirmed requirements for release review

The rules below carry "proposed, owner to confirm" in their source pages. Until the owner confirms one, its text is a proposal: a release gate must not count it as an agreed requirement, and a test written from it must say so. Each row links to its source page. The last column quotes the owner that the source names; "not named" means the source gives none. The sources set no deadline for any of these rules.

Rule What it requires, in short Source page Owner named in source
[LIF-702] End-of-life and abandonment dates are checked on the wall clock at server start and every 1 h; a backward clock jump does not re-enable a retired plugin Lifecycle not named
[LIF-729] A core plugin's third and later failures restart after 5 s; a persistent notice follows after 10 failures in one window Lifecycle not named
[LIF-978] Three crashes during start within 5 minutes in third-party safe mode make the next start use all-optional User safe mode and troubleshooting not named
[LIF-979] Three crashes during start in all-optional make the next start use --no-plugins and open the recovery page first User safe mode and troubleshooting not named
[USR-345] Safe mode is entered by ilium --safe-mode, by ILIUM_SAFE_MODE=1, or after 3 starts in 5 minutes that end in a crash while loading plugins User safe mode and troubleshooting not named
[HST-950] A plugin side is stopped as stopped-by-failure at 5 failures in 24 hours, with no restart scheduled Errors and limits not named
[HST-665] On a network filesystem the lock file is renewed every 10 s and is stale after 60 s; without a safe lock the host starts read-only Plugin files not named
[HST-970] An administrator runs ilium plugin backup at least every 24 hours from a scheduled job that fails loudly Guide, backup and restore not named
[HST-971] An administrator keeps at least the 7 newest archives, on a different disk from the live plugin folder Guide, backup and restore not named
[HST-973] A restore drill runs at least monthly and after every host version change Guide, backup and restore not named
[HST-975] The recovery point objective for plugin data is 24 hours Guide, backup and restore not named
[HST-976] A restore of one plugin's data from an archive up to 1 GiB completes within 15 minutes on the reference machine Guide, backup and restore not named
[DEV-993] Direct upgrade from any supported minor to the next major; a host refuses state written by a host more than one major older with state.too-old This page, Production additions: T9-compat-deprecation not named
[DEV-964] Each host minor gets security fixes for at least 12 months after its release date ABI and major versions not named
[DEV-995] A major host release is announced at least 6 months before its release date, with its removals ABI and major versions not named
[ABI-950] The final 0.x minor stays loadable for 12 months after 2.0.0 ABI and major versions the project maintainer who signs the 1.0.0 release
[ABI-951] The final minor of each major stays loadable for 12 months after the next major ABI and major versions not named
[USR-301] Every built-in theme colour role reaches a contrast ratio of 4.5:1 against the theme background Accessibility and theming not named
[USR-952] The host does not change an operating-system accessibility value a plugin receives; the [ui] value wins when both are set Accessibility and theming not named

The list covers the rules that bear on restart, upgrade, backup and recovery, plus the two examples named in the release review notes: [LIF-702] (end-of-life clock check) and [USR-952] (accessibility settings). Other proposed rules in the manual, such as the registry and developer-tooling rules, are not listed here. To list all of them, search the pages for the phrase owner to confirm.

Downgrading the host after newer data was written

Rolling back the Ilium binary can leave on-disk files that a newer host wrote. This section fixes which files an older host reads and what it does with the rest.

  • [LIF-304] Every on-disk format of the plugin system MUST carry a format number. A host MUST read a file whose format number is at most its own and MUST NOT rewrite a file with a lower number than the one it found.
  • [LIF-305] A host that finds installed.json, a bucket or a stamp with a newer format number than it knows MUST start with the affected plugins disabled, MUST log host.format-newer naming the file, and MUST NOT delete or truncate it, so the operator can run the newer host again without data loss.

Production additions: T9-compat-deprecation

  • [DEV-993] The host MUST support upgrading directly from any supported minor to the next major and from the last minor of a major to any later minor of the next major, and MUST refuse starting on state written by a host more than one major older with state.too-old (proposed, owner to confirm), naming the intermediate version to install.

Requirement statements

  • [LIF-304] Every on-disk format of the plugin system MUST carry a format number. A host MUST read a file whose format number is at most its own and MUST NOT rewrite a file with a lower number than the one it found.
  • [LIF-305] A host that finds installed.json, a bucket or a stamp with a newer format number than it knows MUST start with the affected plugins disabled, MUST log host.format-newer naming the file, and MUST NOT delete or truncate it, so the operator can run the newer host again without data loss.
